contentBody: Which statement best describes generative AI?
option.1: AI that only sorts inputs into predefined fixed categories
option.2: AI that ranks web pages purely by their inbound link counts
option.3: AI that stores and retrieves records from a company database
option.4: AI that creates new content such as text, images, or audio

contentBody: What does the abbreviation LLM stand for in AI?
option.1: Large Language Model
option.2: Linear Logic Method
option.3: Layered Learning Machine
option.4: Long Latency Memory

contentBody: In language models, tokenization is the process of doing what to text?
option.1: Converting the text from one human language to another
option.2: Breaking text into smaller units the model reads
option.3: Encrypting the text so that only the model can decode it
option.4: Compressing the text file to save storage space on disk

contentBody: In the context of LLMs, what is a prompt?
option.1: The internal numeric weights the model has learned
option.2: The hardware chip that runs the model's computations
option.3: The dataset originally used to train the model itself
option.4: The input text or instruction given to the model

contentBody: What best describes a foundation model?
option.1: A model designed solely to store user login details
option.2: A model that runs entirely without any training data
option.3: A small model built to solve only one narrow task
option.4: A model pretrained on broad data for many tasks

contentBody: In LLMs, the term hallucination refers to when the model does what?
option.1: Refuses to answer a question because of its safety filters
option.2: Produces false or fabricated information as if true
option.3: Processes images instead of the usual plain text input
option.4: Runs much slower than expected during heavy server load

contentBody: In text generation, raising the temperature setting generally makes the output more what?
option.1: Quick to compute
option.2: Repetitive and fixed
option.3: Random and varied
option.4: Short in length

contentBody: The context window of an LLM refers to what?
option.1: The screen area where the chat is shown to the users
option.2: The number of users allowed to query the model at once
option.3: The time period the model spent being trained on data
option.4: The amount of text the model can consider at once

contentBody: In machine learning, an embedding is best described as what?
option.1: A numeric vector representation of data like text
option.2: A printed copy of the model's training documents
option.3: A backup file that stores past user conversations
option.4: A rule written by hand to filter out unwanted inputs

contentBody: Giving an LLM a few worked examples inside the prompt before asking it to do a task is called what?
option.1: Zero-shot prompting
option.2: Few-shot prompting
option.3: Fine-tuning the model
option.4: Batch inference

contentBody: In agentic AI, which statement best describes an AI agent?
option.1: A spreadsheet macro that formats numbers inside cells
option.2: A single image classifier with no ability to act
option.3: A system that plans and takes actions to reach a goal
option.4: A static table of questions paired with fixed answers

contentBody: In AI, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) means the model does what?
option.1: Generates replies using only its fixed internal knowledge
option.2: Randomly guesses answers whenever it is unsure of the facts
option.3: Is retrained from scratch each time a user asks something
option.4: Fetches relevant external documents to inform its answer

contentBody: Fine-tuning a pretrained model means doing what?
option.1: Running the model to produce answers for the end users
option.2: Building a brand new model from random initial weights
option.3: Deleting part of the model just to make it smaller in size
option.4: Training it further on a narrower task-specific dataset

contentBody: Using an already-trained model to produce outputs for new inputs is called what?
option.1: Backpropagation
option.2: Inference
option.3: Tokenization
option.4: Training

contentBody: A multimodal AI model is one that can do what?
option.1: Be trained by several different teams at the same time
option.2: Work with several input types like text and images
option.3: Operate only on plain unformatted text input alone
option.4: Run across many computers linked into a cluster

contentBody: In a neural network, the parameters (weights) are best described as what?
option.1: The values learned during training that shape outputs
option.2: The physical memory chips installed inside the computer
option.3: The settings a user picks before starting a chat session
option.4: The raw text prompts typed in by the end user each time

contentBody: Compared with a simple chatbot, an AI agent is better described as one that does what?
option.1: Can take actions and use tools to complete tasks
option.2: Stores far more chat history than a chatbot is able to
option.3: Only replies with text and never performs any action
option.4: Always responds faster than any chatbot ever could

contentBody: Tool calling, also known as function calling, lets an LLM do what?
option.1: Write its own brand new source code and deploy it alone
option.2: Call external functions to act or fetch live data
option.3: Increase the number of parameters it has while running
option.4: Translate its answers into any spoken human language

contentBody: A system prompt in a chat model is typically used to do what?
option.1: Measure how fast the model responds to each request
option.2: Count the total number of tokens used in a session
option.3: Set the assistant's overall behavior and rules
option.4: Store the entire history of every past conversation

contentBody: In an LLM interaction, the text the model generates in response to the prompt is called the what?
option.1: Embedding
option.2: Checkpoint
option.3: Parameter
option.4: Completion

contentBody: In a transformer, what does the self-attention mechanism primarily allow the model to do when processing a sequence?
option.1: Encode the whole sequence into a single fixed vector before the first layer runs
option.2: Let each token gather information from other tokens, weighted by their relevance
option.3: Swap each token for its closest dictionary synonym to normalize the input text first
option.4: Read tokens strictly left to right, never comparing one token against another one

contentBody: A standard autoregressive language model generates text by doing what at each step?
option.1: Selecting a full sentence from a fixed list of memorized candidate responses each time
option.2: Predicting a probability distribution over the next token given all preceding tokens
option.3: Filling in randomly masked tokens spread throughout the complete input sequence at once
option.4: Predicting every token in the output sentence at once in a single parallel forward pass

contentBody: Why do transformer language models have a finite context window rather than accepting unlimited input length?
option.1: The output layer can emit just a fixed number of tokens, which caps the input length too
option.2: Attention compute scales with length and training used a fixed maximum length
option.3: The model keeps only one sentence in memory and throws away all earlier text later
option.4: Longer inputs are blocked because tokenization can handle only a few hundred characters

contentBody: Byte pair encoding and similar subword tokenizers split rare words into smaller pieces mainly to achieve what?
option.1: Translate the input into another language before the model begins its processing
option.2: Represent any word, including unseen ones, with a fixed, manageable vocabulary
option.3: Remove all punctuation and spacing so the model sees only lowercase letter runs later
option.4: Guarantee that each individual English word maps to exactly one whole-word token

contentBody: In semantic search, why is cosine similarity between embedding vectors used to compare two texts?
option.1: It measures the exact character-level edit distance between the two input strings
option.2: Cosine similarity counts how many identical words the two texts literally share
option.3: Texts with similar meaning map to vectors pointing in similar directions
option.4: Shorter texts always score higher because the vector magnitude becomes much smaller

contentBody: Retrieval-augmented generation reduces hallucination primarily because it does what?
option.1: Retrains the model weights on the user question before producing any final answer
option.2: Lowers the sampling temperature to zero so the model can never make any mistake
option.3: Supplies relevant retrieved documents so answers can be grounded in real text
option.4: Removes the language model entirely and just returns raw search hits to the user

contentBody: Why are long documents usually split into smaller chunks before being indexed for retrieval?
option.1: Smaller passages match queries more precisely and fit the context budget
option.2: Each chunk is translated separately, which improves the overall writing style later
option.3: Chunking permanently compresses the text so storage cost drops to almost nothing
option.4: The vector database rejects any document longer than a single short paragraph

contentBody: What is the primary role of a vector database in a retrieval system?
option.1: Store embeddings and quickly find those nearest to a query vector
option.2: Convert user questions into SQL and run them against relational tables first
option.3: Generate the final natural language answer shown directly to the end user
option.4: Compress the model weights so the language model loads faster at startup time

contentBody: Chain-of-thought prompting tends to improve performance on multi-step reasoning tasks because it does what?
option.1: Retrieves external documents that already contain the fully worked out solution
option.2: Forces the model to answer only in a single word so there is no confusion
option.3: Prompts the model to lay out intermediate steps before giving the answer
option.4: Increases the sampling temperature so the model explores far more creative guesses

contentBody: What distinguishes few-shot prompting from zero-shot prompting?
option.1: Few-shot always uses a higher sampling temperature than zero-shot prompting does
option.2: Few-shot works only for images, while zero-shot applies just to plain text tasks
option.3: Few-shot includes worked examples in the prompt while zero-shot gives none
option.4: Few-shot permanently updates the model weights, while zero-shot leaves them fixed

contentBody: In a chat-formatted prompt, what is the typical purpose of the system role message?
option.1: Set the overall behavior and constraints for the assistant
option.2: Store the retrieved documents that were fetched from an external knowledge base
option.3: Hold the model's previous replies so they can be echoed back to the user later
option.4: Contain the exact question the end user is asking on this current turn

contentBody: Why might a developer instruct a model to return its output as strict JSON?
option.1: So downstream code can parse the fields reliably without fragile scraping
option.2: Because JSON responses are always shorter than the equivalent plain English answers
option.3: Because JSON output makes the language model reason more accurately on hard problems
option.4: Because JSON output can never contain any factual mistakes or invented information

contentBody: How do temperature and top-p sampling differ in how they control randomness during generation?
option.1: Temperature edits the prompt wording, while top-p changes the model architecture
option.2: Temperature sets the output length, while top-p selects the language of the response
option.3: Temperature rescales the logits; top-p keeps only the top probability mass
option.4: Both are identical settings, so changing either one has exactly the same effect anyway

contentBody: When a RAG system attaches citations to its answer, what does this primarily let a user do?
option.1: Confirm that the language model was retrained on the very latest available data
option.2: See how long the model spent generating each sentence of the final response here
option.3: Check the answer against the specific source passages that were retrieved
option.4: Guarantee the answer is correct because any cited answer is automatically true

contentBody: Prompt injection is best described as an attack in which what happens?
option.1: Malicious text in the input tricks the model into ignoring its instructions
option.2: Random noise is added to embeddings so retrieval returns unrelated documents instead
option.3: The database server is overloaded with traffic until it stops responding at all
option.4: Model weights are stolen and copied onto an attacker controlled server remotely

contentBody: Reinforcement learning from human feedback is primarily used to do what to a language model?
option.1: Expand its context window so it can read much longer documents at once
option.2: Align its responses with human preferences about helpfulness and safety
option.3: Teach it an entirely new natural language it was never exposed to before
option.4: Compress its parameters so it runs on much smaller devices than usual now

contentBody: What is the core idea behind parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA?
option.1: Delete unused layers so the network becomes smaller and faster to serve later
option.2: Replace the tokenizer with a custom one tailored to the target domain data set
option.3: Retrain every parameter of the base model from scratch on the new dataset
option.4: Train a small set of added weights while keeping the base model frozen

contentBody: For giving a model access to a frequently changing knowledge base, why is RAG often preferred over fine-tuning?
option.1: RAG permanently bakes the facts into the weights so no storage is needed later on
option.2: Fine-tuning is the only method that can ever change how the model behaves at all
option.3: Fine-tuning updates the stored knowledge automatically every time a document changes
option.4: New documents can be indexed instantly without retraining the model weights

contentBody: In an LLM, where does knowledge supplied at inference time through the prompt reside, versus knowledge learned during training?
option.1: Both kinds live only in the prompt and vanish as soon as the current request completes
option.2: Both kinds of knowledge are stored permanently inside the model weight matrices only
option.3: Prompt knowledge sits in the context window; trained knowledge is in the weights
option.4: Prompt knowledge is saved to disk, while trained knowledge stays inside the prompt text

contentBody: In a retrieval pipeline, what is the purpose of a re-ranking step after the initial search?
option.1: Generate brand new documents to add into the knowledge base automatically now
option.2: Reorder candidates so the most relevant passages rise to the top
option.3: Delete the vector database once the first set of results has been fetched
option.4: Translate every retrieved passage into the language used by the question

contentBody: What primarily distinguishes an agentic system from a single, one-shot LLM call?
option.1: It relies on a much larger model with many billions more parameters than a chatbot
option.2: It handles the user request without ever calling a language model at all
option.3: It can invoke tools, observe the results, and choose its next step toward a goal
option.4: It always returns longer and more detailed prose than a normal chat response

contentBody: In the perceive-reason-act loop, what does the perceive step mainly provide to the agent?
option.1: The current observations or environment state used to decide what to do next
option.2: A randomly chosen tool that the agent must execute before doing anything else
option.3: A rewrite of the agent's own system prompt to change its overall personality
option.4: A final committed answer that ends the loop and stops all further processing

contentBody: How does an LLM typically make use of an external tool during function calling?
option.1: It emits a structured request naming the tool and arguments; a runtime runs it
option.2: It permanently compiles the tool into the model's parameters before using it
option.3: It guesses the tool's output from context instead of actually invoking it at all
option.4: It executes the selected tool's code directly within its own neural network weights

contentBody: The ReAct pattern is characterized by which approach to reasoning and acting?
option.1: Generating one complete final answer up front before ever taking any action
option.2: Avoiding tool use entirely and reasoning purely from memorized training facts
option.3: Taking several random actions first and only reasoning about the outcomes afterward
option.4: Interleaving reasoning steps with actions so each thought guides the next call

contentBody: In an agent, what does task decomposition (planning) primarily involve?
option.1: Discarding steps from a task so the agent can finish the whole thing more quickly
option.2: Translating the user's original request into a different natural language first
option.3: Splitting a complex goal into smaller subtasks the agent can tackle in order
option.4: Compressing several separate user requests into a single very short summary line

contentBody: In an agent, short-term (working) memory typically holds which of the following?
option.1: The recent context of the current task, such as intermediate results and dialogue
option.2: The model's fixed pretrained weights, which never change at runtime during a task
option.3: User preferences stored indefinitely so they can be recalled in future sessions
option.4: Permanent facts retrieved from an external database and reused across many sessions

contentBody: Why do multi-step agents generally need some form of memory?
option.1: So the underlying language model can permanently update its own weights during a run
option.2: So the agent can produce answers without ever having to call any external tools
option.3: So every new step starts completely fresh with no knowledge of what came before
option.4: So results and decisions from earlier steps stay available to inform later ones

contentBody: What is the orchestrator in an agent system mainly responsible for?
option.1: Storing the user's password and other secret credentials in an encrypted vault
option.2: Coordinating the flow between steps, tools, and models toward the overall goal
option.3: Computing the raw token probabilities for every individual word the model produces
option.4: Rendering the agent's final answer as a formatted web page for the end user

contentBody: When is a fixed, deterministic workflow usually preferable to an autonomous agent?
option.1: When the task is open ended and the necessary steps cannot be known ahead of time
option.2: When the inputs vary so widely that no two runs ever look remotely similar at all
option.3: When the goal keeps changing and requires fresh creative reasoning on every run
option.4: When the steps are known and fixed, so predictability and low cost matter most

contentBody: What is a human-in-the-loop checkpoint in an agent primarily used for?
option.1: Replacing the language model entirely with a person who writes every response
option.2: Getting human approval before the agent performs a risky or irreversible action
option.3: Letting the agent run much faster by skipping any and all review of its planned actions
option.4: Hiding the agent's reasoning so that users cannot see how decisions were made

contentBody: What does a reflection or self-critique step let an agent do?
option.1: Delete all memory of the task so that it can restart again from scratch
option.2: Increase the size of the model it runs on partway through a single task
option.3: Skip all verification and return its very first draft as quickly as possible
option.4: Review its own draft output, spot errors, and revise it before finalizing

contentBody: What is a key risk when an agent must choose among many available tools?
option.1: It runs every available tool at the same time and safely merges all of the outputs
option.2: It becomes permanently unable to produce any text output for the rest of the session
option.3: It may pick the wrong tool or pass incorrect arguments, producing a faulty result
option.4: It permanently deletes any tools that it decides it does not need for the current task

contentBody: Why are agent tools usually described with structured schemas, such as JSON with typed parameters?
option.1: So the model knows each tool's inputs and can format valid, checkable calls
option.2: So that the tool can run without any code ever being written by a developer
option.3: So that users are forced to memorize every parameter name before using the agent
option.4: So the model can ignore the parameters and call the tools however it likes

contentBody: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is best described as which of the following?
option.1: A compression format used for shrinking a model's weights before it is deployed
option.2: A ranking system that scores which chatbot gives the best answers to a prompt
option.3: A training technique that makes language models substantially larger and more accurate
option.4: A standard interface that lets models connect to external tools and data sources

contentBody: What is a common reason to use several specialized agents instead of one general agent?
option.1: Each agent can focus on a narrow role, so its part is easier to design and check
option.2: A single agent is physically incapable of ever calling more than one tool at a time
option.3: Multiple agents remove any need to define an overall goal for the whole system
option.4: Adding more and more agents will always guarantee a faster and cheaper final result

contentBody: In a multi-step agent, what does the state passed between steps usually refer to?
option.1: The total number of times the user has opened the application during this month
option.2: The model's internal pretrained weights being edited after each individual step
option.3: The physical server location where the agent's process happens to be running now
option.4: The accumulated results carried forward so later steps can build on them

contentBody: Grounding an agent's actions in real data, for example through retrieval, mainly helps to do what?
option.1: Let the agent completely avoid using any tools while still sounding confident
option.2: Increase the creativity of its answers by ignoring the provided factual data
option.3: Make the agent respond faster by skipping any external data lookups
option.4: Base its outputs on verifiable sources instead of unsupported guesses

contentBody: Why is a stopping condition added to an agent loop?
option.1: To guarantee the agent uses each of its available tools an equal number of times
option.2: To end the loop when the goal is met or a step limit is hit, avoiding endless runs
option.3: To force the model to produce much longer answers on every single attempt it makes
option.4: To prevent the agent from ever asking the user any clarifying question at all

contentBody: Compared with a single LLM call, a multi-step agent typically exhibits which trade-off?
option.1: No way to make use of external tools during any part of its execution flow
option.2: Lower accuracy on every task because the extra steps only ever add confusion
option.3: Higher cost and latency, since each step adds more model calls and tokens
option.4: A completely fixed runtime that never changes no matter how hard the task becomes

contentBody: After an agent executes an action, what normally happens to the resulting observation?
option.1: It is discarded right away so that it cannot influence any later decisions
option.2: It is used to permanently retrain the underlying base model before continuing
option.3: It is fed back into the loop so the next reasoning step can account for it
option.4: It is shown only to the end user and is never seen by the agent again

contentBody: In a planner-executor agent architecture, what is the primary reason for separating planning from execution rather than deciding and acting in one combined loop?
option.1: Separating decomposition from action lets the planner reason over the whole task upfront, so the executor runs steps without re-deriving the goal each time.
option.2: It makes the whole system deterministic, because fixing the plan also fixes the exact tokens the executor will emit at every later step.
option.3: It guarantees the plan cannot fail, because every step is fully validated against the goal before any action in the environment is ever run.
option.4: It removes the executor's need to call external tools, since the planner resolves and pre-computes all of the required tool calls in advance.

contentBody: The reflection (self-critique) pattern, where an agent reviews and revises its own prior output, most reliably improves performance on tasks with which property?
option.1: The model has no access to any tools, which usefully forces it to rely on internal reasoning alone when producing the revised answer.
option.2: The task provides a checkable signal of correctness the critique can use, such as test results, error messages, or verifiable constraints.
option.3: The task is purely subjective, so any self-generated critique is just as valid as an external judgment about whether the output is right.
option.4: The final answer is a single token, which minimizes the chance of the revision step introducing brand new errors into the output.

contentBody: What is the essential capability that tree-of-thoughts adds over a single chain-of-thought?
option.1: It removes the need for any intermediate reasoning by producing the final answer directly from the prompt in a single decoding pass.
option.2: It guarantees a globally optimal solution by exhaustively enumerating every possible thought before it selects one final answer to return.
option.3: It replaces the underlying language model with a symbolic search engine that no longer samples tokens from a learned distribution.
option.4: It explores multiple reasoning branches and can backtrack, abandoning unpromising partial solutions instead of committing to one linear path.

contentBody: In multi-agent systems, what best distinguishes orchestration from choreography?
option.1: Orchestration requires every agent to share one common model, while choreography strictly requires each agent to run a distinct and separate model.
option.2: Orchestration permits agents to use external tools, while choreography by definition forbids any agent from calling external tools at all.
option.3: Orchestration uses a central coordinator that directs each agent, while in choreography agents react to shared events or messages with no central controller.
option.4: Orchestration is always synchronous while choreography is always asynchronous, and this timing contrast is what defines the two patterns apart.

contentBody: In a long multi-step agent task where each dependent step succeeds independently with probability p, why does end-to-end reliability often degrade faster than practitioners expect?
option.1: The model forgets its system prompt after a fixed number of steps, which triggers one abrupt failure late in the otherwise reliable task.
option.2: Errors made in separate steps tend to cancel out over a long run, so the real risk is underconfidence rather than any compounding of failures.
option.3: Latency accumulates roughly linearly across the steps, and this growing delay is the dominant cause of end-to-end task failure over time.
option.4: Per-step success probabilities multiply, so even individually high reliability yields a product that falls sharply as the chain of dependent steps grows.

contentBody: Why is evaluating an agent generally harder than evaluating a single LLM response?
option.1: Only the final answer matters for an agent, so its intermediate tool calls can be safely ignored during any careful scoring process.
option.2: Agent outputs are fully deterministic, which removes the evaluator's ability to sample and compare multiple gradings of the same run.
option.3: Agents always produce much longer text, so an evaluator simply needs more tokens of surrounding context to grade the response accurately.
option.4: An agent produces a trajectory of interdependent actions, so correctness depends on the whole path and its side effects, not on one final string.

contentBody: In advanced RAG, what is the main reason to combine dense (vector) retrieval with sparse (keyword) retrieval before a re-ranking stage?
option.1: Sparse retrieval captures meaning while dense retrieval only matches exact strings, so pairing them conveniently covers both retrieval needs at once.
option.2: Combining the two removes any need for a re-ranking stage, because their union is already ordered perfectly by relevance to the input query.
option.3: Dense retrieval captures semantic similarity while sparse retrieval catches exact terms like rare IDs, so together they raise recall before re-ranking.
option.4: Dense and sparse retrieval return essentially identical candidate sets, so the combination mainly adds redundancy that improves overall reliability.

contentBody: Under which condition does putting all documents directly into a long context window tend to beat retrieval-augmented generation?
option.1: When the corpus is small enough to fit in context and reasoning needs information scattered across many parts that retrieval might fragment or miss.
option.2: When the cost per query must be minimized, since sending a full long context is always cheaper than running a separate retrieval step.
option.3: When exact keyword lookup is required, because a long context window performs literal string matching more reliably than a retriever does.
option.4: When the corpus is far larger than any context window, since long context scales gracefully to an effectively unlimited number of documents.

contentBody: What is the core idea that distinguishes GraphRAG from standard chunk-based RAG?
option.1: It guarantees that every retrieved fact is correct, because each edge in the graph is verified against an authoritative external database first.
option.2: It stores document chunks as image graphs so that a vision model can read and scan through the material faster than it could read plain text.
option.3: It builds a structured graph of entities and relationships from the corpus, so retrieval can traverse connections and answer questions that span many documents.
option.4: It replaces the language model with a graph neural network that answers questions directly from edges without any text generation step at all.

contentBody: For a tool-using agent that reads untrusted web content, which is the most robust defense against prompt injection?
option.1: Add a strong system prompt that instructs the model to never follow any instructions that appear inside the retrieved external content it reads.
option.2: Treat retrieved content as untrusted data and constrain the actions the agent may take on it, not just instruct the model to ignore malicious text.
option.3: Increase the model size, since sufficiently large models become effectively immune to instructions injected through tool outputs and web pages.
option.4: Encrypt the retrieved content before use, so that any injected instructions inside it cannot be parsed or acted on by the model at all.

contentBody: Why is exact reproducibility difficult to guarantee for LLM-based agents even at temperature zero?
option.1: Greedy decoding always yields byte-identical text on every machine, so any observed variation must be the result of a bug in the harness.
option.2: The model retrains itself on each incoming query, so its underlying weights are different by the time the next identical request arrives to it.
option.3: Temperature zero still samples randomly from the full distribution, so the produced text is expected to vary from one run to the next by design.
option.4: Nondeterministic GPU floating-point reductions, and tool or environment state that changes between runs, can alter outputs even under greedy decoding.

contentBody: In a long-horizon agent task that ends in failure, why is credit assignment particularly hard?
option.1: Failure in a long task is always caused by the final action taken, so only that last step ever needs to be inspected to explain the outcome.
option.2: The failure may stem from an early decision whose consequences only surfaced many steps later, making it hard to attribute the outcome to the responsible action.
option.3: Every step in the trajectory contributes exactly equally to the outcome, so blame for the failure can simply be divided uniformly across steps.
option.4: The reward signal is dense at every single step, so the action responsible for the eventual failure is immediately obvious from the trace.

contentBody: An agent sometimes calls a valid tool but with fabricated argument values. Which mitigation most directly addresses this?
option.1: Validate arguments against the tool schema and known valid values before running, then re-prompt or reject when a value cannot be grounded.
option.2: Give the model access to many more tools, so that it always has alternatives available whenever one particular call happens to fail at runtime.
option.3: Raise the sampling temperature, so that the model considers a wider and more creative range of possible argument values on each attempt it makes.
option.4: Remove the tool schema entirely, so that the model is free to choose whatever argument names and formats it prefers for each separate call.

contentBody: What does a standard agent-tool protocol such as the Model Context Protocol primarily aim to solve compared with ad-hoc function calling?
option.1: It defines a common interface so tools and data sources can be reused across different agents and hosts without bespoke integration for each pairing.
option.2: It makes every tool call run faster by compiling the supplied function definitions down into native machine code before the agent executes them.
option.3: It removes the need for the model to decide which tool to call, because the protocol itself selects the correct tool automatically for the agent.
option.4: It guarantees that any tool connected through the protocol is secure and structurally incapable of leaking the data it is given access to.

contentBody: Increasing an agent's autonomy by removing human-in-the-loop checkpoints has which characteristic tradeoff?
option.1: Throughput and speed rise while the cost of undetected errors grows, since fewer points remain to catch mistakes before they cause irreversible effects.
option.2: Both error rates and latency fall together, because the human review stage was in practice the only real source of mistakes in the pipeline.
option.3: Reproducibility improves substantially, because removing the human from the loop is what makes the overall system behave fully deterministically.
option.4: The agent then needs fewer tools, because greater autonomy reduces the total number of distinct actions it is ever able to take on a task.

contentBody: Why might placing guardrails only on the final output of a tool-using agent be insufficient?
option.1: The input and tool-call layers cannot be inspected at runtime, so checking the final output is the only technically feasible option available.
option.2: Tool actions can cause harmful or unauthorized effects during execution, so unsafe behavior must also be caught at the input and tool-call layers.
option.3: Output guardrails noticeably slow down generation, so relocating them earlier in the pipeline is purely a latency optimization with no safety change.
option.4: A well-aligned model always produces safe final outputs, so placing guardrails on those outputs is largely redundant work that can be removed.

contentBody: What distinguishes agentic RAG from a standard retrieve-then-generate pipeline?
option.1: The agent decides dynamically whether, when, and what to retrieve, and can issue multiple targeted queries or skip retrieval based on the evolving task.
option.2: It retrieves exactly once at the very start of the task and then never issues another query for the remainder of the interaction with the user.
option.3: It removes the generation step altogether and returns the retrieved passages verbatim to the user as the complete answer to their question.
option.4: It always retrieves a fixed number of chunks before generating anything, which ensures the context size stays consistent across every possible query.

contentBody: In an open-ended agent loop, which strategy most directly controls runaway cost without simply degrading the underlying model?
option.1: Always switch to the single largest available model, since its stronger reasoning tends to finish any given task in far fewer overall steps.
option.2: Increase the sampling temperature, so the agent explores a broader set of candidate solutions on every single iteration of the outer loop.
option.3: Impose explicit budgets such as step, token, or tool-call limits with a stopping rule, so the loop halts once it passes a defined threshold.
option.4: Remove all stopping conditions, so the agent is free to discover the cheapest possible path entirely on its own over the course of the run.

contentBody: What is the key correctness precondition for safely caching (memoising) an agent's tool call results?
option.1: The tool must be slow to run, since only expensive calls are ever worth caching regardless of how the tool actually behaves internally each time.
option.2: The tool must modify some external state on every call, so that the cache can faithfully record each of those state changes for later replay.
option.3: The tool must be effectively deterministic and free of side effects for a given input, so a stored result stays valid whenever it is reused.
option.4: The tool must return a genuinely different result on each call, which is what ensures the contents of the cache always stay fresh over time.

contentBody: Why does inserting verification or grounding steps between actions help most in long agent trajectories?
option.1: It guarantees the final answer is correct, because every step in the trajectory was independently checked before the agent moved onward.
option.2: Catching and correcting an error early prevents it from propagating and compounding through later dependent steps, keeping the trajectory on track.
option.3: It makes each individual step run faster, and that speedup is the main way the added verification improves the final accuracy of the task.
option.4: It removes the need for any planning at all, since steps that have been verified along the way no longer require an overall plan to succeed.
